usage: 볼펜 좀 빌려주세요
Lend me a pen, please
Everyday request at a desk or counter; 좀 softens it into a polite favor
검은색 볼펜으로 써 주세요
Please write with a black pen
Banks and offices often require 검은색 (black); 으로 marks the pen as the tool you write with
볼펜이 안 나와요
The pen isn't writing
안 나오다 (won't come out) is THE idiom for a dead pen — the ink won't flow
볼펜 어디 있어요?
Where's a pen?
Casual workplace ask; in speech Koreans drop the 이/가 subject marker after 볼펜
examples: 볼펜 하나만 빌려도 돼요?
Can I just borrow one pen?
Simplest favor; 하나만 = just one, -아/어도 돼요? asks permission gently
여기에 볼펜으로 이름을 쓰시면 됩니다.
You can write your name here with a pen
-으로 marks the tool you write with
회의 때 쓸 볼펜이 한 자루도 없네요.
There isn't a single pen to use in the meeting.
Real frustration; 자루 counts pens, and 한 자루도 없다 = not even one
nuance: 볼펜 is a loanword shortened from English 'ball pen' and means specifically a ballpoint, the cheap everyday pen, whereas plain 펜 is the umbrella word for any pen and would also cover a 만년필 (fountain pen) or 사인펜 (felt-tip marker). Koreans default to 볼펜 for ordinary office pens and only switch to those other words when the type matters. The near-synonym 사인펜 is NOT a 'sign pen' for signing — it is a felt-tip; you sign with a 볼펜. Pair 볼펜 with 으로 to mean 'with a pen' (볼펜으로 쓰다), count it with the writing-implement counter 자루, and remember the English-speaker trap: a dead pen is 볼펜이 안 나와요 (the ink won't come out), not the literal 안 써져요, which sounds slightly off to natives.

Calling a felt-tip 사인펜 a signing pen by false-friend logic — 사인펜 is a marker; you actually sign with a 볼펜
Counting pens with the generic 개 in writing; the natural counter is 자루, as in 볼펜 한 자루

usage: 노트에 적어 두세요
Jot it down in your notebook
적어 두다 = write it down and keep it; the go-to phrase for taking a note for later
노트 필기 좀 보여 줄래?
Can you show me your notes?
필기 = handwritten class/meeting notes; -ㄹ래? is a casual peer request
새 노트 한 권 샀어요
I bought a new notebook
권 is the book counter and the natural one for a bound notebook
노트 정리가 깔끔하네요
Your notes are neatly organized
정리 = organizing; a common compliment about tidy, well-kept notes
examples: 노트에 이름을 써 주세요.
Please write your name in the notebook.
Simple classroom line; 에 marks the notebook as where the writing lands
회의 내용을 노트에 다 적었어요.
I wrote down everything from the meeting in my notebook.
Everyday work use; 다 적다 = jot it all down
디지털 노트보다 종이 노트가 더 편해요.
I find a paper notebook more comfortable than a digital one.
Real preference talk; A보다 B가 더 = B is more ~ than A
nuance: 노트 is a loanword from English 'note(book)' but in Korean it means the physical bound pad you write in, NOT an abstract 'note' or 'memo' (that idea is 메모). The dangerous near-homophone is 노트북, which to a Korean ear means a laptop computer 100% of the time, never a paper notebook — so the single syllable 북 completely changes the object. There is also 공책 (空冊, 'empty book'), the older textbook word for a school notebook, but adults overwhelmingly say 노트 in daily and office life, and 메모지 covers small loose notepaper instead. Count a 노트 with 권 (the book counter), pair it with 적다/필기하다, and never assume 노트 = your to-do 'notes'; for a quick reminder Koreans say 메모.

Using 노트 to translate an abstract 'a note to self'; that idea is 메모, and 노트 is the physical book
Counting notebooks with 개; the natural counter is 권, as in 노트 한 권

usage: 테이프로 붙여 주세요
Please stick it down with tape
로 marks tape as the tool; 붙이다 = to stick something on
박스테이프 어디 있어요?
Where's the packing tape?
박스테이프 = the wide brown box tape, the one everyone hunts for when moving
테이프가 잘 안 떨어져요
The tape won't come off easily
떨어지다 here = come off; a common complaint when tape over-sticks
투명 테이프로 고정했어요
I fixed it with clear tape
투명 = transparent; 고정하다 = to fasten in place
examples: 테이프로 좀 붙여 주세요.
Please tape it up for me.
Simplest request; 좀 softens it and 붙이다 carries the 'stick' meaning
택배 상자를 테이프로 단단히 붙였어요.
I sealed the delivery box tightly with tape.
Everyday shipping/moving; 단단히 = firmly, securely
양면테이프가 일반 테이프보다 훨씬 잘 붙어요.
Double-sided tape sticks much better than regular tape.
Real comparison; 훨씬 = far/much more, and here 붙다 = (it) sticks
nuance: 테이프 is a loanword from English 'tape' and covers most sticky tapes, but Koreans habitually name the type: 박스테이프 (packing tape), 투명 테이프 or 스카치테이프 (clear desk tape, from the Scotch brand), and 양면테이프 (double-sided). The crucial English-speaker trap is transitivity: to stick something on, use the transitive 붙이다 (테이프로 붙이다 = stick it with tape); the intransitive 붙다 means '(it) sticks/is stuck' and can't take an object, so 테이프를 붙다 is wrong. Note the pair flips by viewpoint — 테이프로 종이를 붙이다 (I stick the paper) vs 테이프가 잘 붙다 (the tape sticks well). Don't import the English verb 'tape' as 테이프하다 either; the action is always carried by 붙이다.

Calling clear desk tape 박스테이프; the wide brown tape is only for boxes, while desk tape is 투명 테이프/스카치테이프

usage: 스테이플러로 찍어 주세요
Please staple it together
찍다 (to stamp/punch) is the verb for stapling; 로 marks the stapler as the tool
스테이플러 심 다 떨어졌어요
The staples have run out
심 = the staple refills; 떨어지다 = run out of a supply
서류 두 장 스테이플러로 찍을게요
I'll staple these two pages
장 counts sheets of paper; -ㄹ게요 = I'll do it (announcing your action)
스테이플러 좀 써도 돼요?
Can I use the stapler?
Polite borrowing in a shared office; -아/어도 돼요? asks permission
examples: 스테이플러로 찍어 줄래요?
Could you staple it for me?
Short favor; the core collocation 스테이플러로 찍다 in a casual -ㄹ래요? request
보고서를 출력해서 스테이플러로 찍었어요.
I printed the report and stapled it.
Typical office flow; 출력하다 = print out, then staple
스테이플러가 자꾸 걸려서 잘 안 찍혀요.
The stapler keeps jamming, so it doesn't staple well.
Real annoyance; 걸리다 = jam/catch, 찍히다 = get stapled (passive)
nuance: 스테이플러 is a loanword from English 'stapler', but the action is pure native Korean: you 찍다 it — a verb whose base sense is to stamp, punch, or press down — so '스테이플러로 찍다' is the only natural collocation and there is NO verb 스테이플러하다. This 찍다 is the same one used for stamping a seal (도장을 찍다) and taking a photo (사진을 찍다), all sharing the 'press down to make a mark' image. The metal staples loaded inside are called 심 — the very same word for pencil 'lead' and mechanical-pencil refills — so 스테이플러 심 다 떨어졌어요 means the staples ran out. English speakers also confuse the device with what it makes: the machine is the 스테이플러, but the individual fastener it leaves is a 스테이플 / 침; in everyday speech the refills are just 심.

usage: 포스트잇에 메모해서 붙여 놨어요
I wrote a memo on a Post-it and stuck it up
메모하다 = jot a memo; 붙여 놓다 = stick it and leave it there
포스트잇 한 장 줄래요?
Can you give me one Post-it?
장 counts the sheets; casual -ㄹ래요? request
모니터에 포스트잇 붙이지 마세요
Don't stick Post-its on the monitor
A real security rule in many offices; -지 마세요 = please don't
포스트잇으로 표시해 뒀어요
I marked it with a Post-it
표시하다 = to flag/mark; 으로 marks the Post-it as the means
examples: 포스트잇 한 장 붙여 주세요.
Please stick on one Post-it.
Simplest task; 한 장 = one sheet, 붙이다 = stick it on
할 일을 포스트잇에 적어서 책상에 붙여요.
I write my to-dos on Post-its and stick them on my desk.
Everyday habit; 할 일 = to-do, 에 marks both surfaces
중요한 페이지마다 포스트잇을 붙여 두세요.
Put a Post-it on every important page.
Practical study/work tip; 마다 = on every, 붙여 두다 = stick and keep
nuance: 포스트잇 became the everyday Korean word for a sticky note even though it began as the 3M brand 'Post-it' — a genericized trademark exactly like 'Post-it' or 'Kleenex' in English. The fully Korean coinage 접착 메모지 (接着 메모지, 'adhesive notepaper') does exist but sounds stiff and bureaucratic, so almost nobody says it aloud; at any office or stationery shop you simply say 포스트잇. Keep it distinct from its neighbors: 메모지 is plain loose notepaper with no stickiness, and 노트 is a bound notebook — only the 포스트잇 self-adheres. Count the slips with 장 (the flat-sheet counter), not 개, and pair it with 붙이다 (stick on), 적다 (write), or 표시하다 (flag). The trap is over-formalizing in casual talk; 접착식 메모지 will sound oddly textbook-ish when 포스트잇 is universal.

usage: 클립으로 묶어 주세요
Please clip them together
묶다 = bind/bundle; 으로 marks the clip as the tool
서류 클립 좀 빼 줄래요?
Can you take the clip off the documents?
빼다 = remove/pull out; casual office ask
클립이 다 어디 갔지?
Where did all the clips go?
Self-talk; -지? muses to oneself, and clips always seem to vanish
클립 말고 집게가 더 나아요
A binder clip is better than a paper clip
말고 = not ~ but; contrasts 클립 vs 집게 (binder clip)
examples: 서류를 클립으로 묶어 주세요.
Please clip the documents together.
Plain request; the core pair 클립으로 묶다
영수증을 클립으로 묶어서 보관했어요.
I clipped the receipts together and kept them.
Everyday filing; 보관하다 = store/keep
페이지가 많아서 클립 대신 스테이플러를 썼어요.
There were many pages, so I used a stapler instead of a clip.
Real decision; 대신 = instead of
nuance: 클립 is a loanword from English 'clip', but on its own it means specifically the small bent-wire paper clip (you can spell it out as 종이 클립). The bigger black fold-back clip with two metal arms is a different object that English calls a 'binder clip'; in Korean that is 집게 ('pincer/tongs') or 더블클립, so you must specify when you need the strong one — 집게 grips far harder than a flimsy 클립. As with other tools there is no verb 클립하다; pair the noun with native verbs instead: 클립으로 묶다 (bind with a clip) or 클립을 끼우다 (slip a clip on). Note the everyday gripe 클립이 서로 달라붙다 (the clips cling to each other) — 달라붙다 = stick together — and remember that to remove one you 빼다 it.

usage: 서류를 파일에 정리했어요
I organized the documents in a folder
정리하다 = sort/organize; 에 marks the folder as the destination
이 파일에 끼워 두세요
Slip it into this file
끼우다 = insert between; 두다 = leave it there for later
클리어파일 하나 주세요
Give me one clear file, please
클리어파일 = the clear-sleeve folder, the most common office kind
파일이 너무 두꺼워졌어요
The file has gotten too thick
두꺼워지다 = become thick; it's stuffed full of papers
examples: 서류를 이 파일에 넣어 주세요.
Please put the documents in this folder.
Simple instruction; 넣다 = put in, 에 = into
중요한 서류를 파일에 넣어서 책장에 꽂아 뒀어요.
I put the important papers in a file and shelved them
파일에 넣다 = put into a folder/file
서류가 많으면 파일로 정리하는 게 편해요.
If you have lots of documents, organizing them in files is convenient.
Advice; -는 게 편하다 = it's convenient to ~
nuance: 파일 is a loanword from English 'file' and is a true homonym: it means both a physical document folder AND a computer file, so only context tells them apart — 파일에 끼우다 (slip into a folder) is clearly the paper kind, while 파일을 저장하다 (save the file) is clearly digital. Within the physical sense, Koreans distinguish sub-types you should not blur: a 클리어파일 is the thin transparent sleeve folder most desks use, whereas a 바인더 is the thick ring binder that snaps open, and a plain 폴더 often refers to the cardboard folder. The English-speaker trap is assuming 파일 defaults to 'computer file' and calling the clear sleeve a 바인더 — but 바인더 specifically has rings. Pair it with 넣다 (put in), 끼우다 (insert), 정리하다 (organize), and 꽂다 (shelve).

usage: 스캐너로 스캔해 주세요
Please scan it with the scanner
스캔하다 = to scan; 로 marks the scanner as the device
스캐너가 어디에 있어요?
Where is the scanner?
Locating shared office equipment; 에 marks the location
서류 좀 스캐너로 떠 줄래요?
Can you scan the document for me?
뜨다 ('lift/take off') is colloquial office slang for scanning a copy
스캐너 연결이 안 돼요
The scanner won't connect
연결이 안 되다 = fails to connect; a typical tech complaint
examples: 이거 스캐너로 스캔해 주세요.
Please scan this with the scanner.
Plainest request; 이거 = this one, plus the core pair 스캐너로 스캔하다
